Exploring Historical Information for RGBE Visual Tracking with Mamba
Chuanyu Sun1*, Jiqing Zhang2*, Yang Wang1, Huilin Ge3†, Qianchen Xia4†, Baocai Yin1,5†, Xin Yang1†
1Key Laboratory of Social Computing and Cognitive Intelligence, Dalian University of Technology
2Dalian Maritime University
3Jiangsu University of Science and Technology
4The Future Laboratory,Tsinghua University, Beijing, China
5Beijing University of Technology
Abstract
Combining the advantages of conventional and event
cameras for robust visual tracing has drawn extensive inter-
est. However, existing tracking approaches heavily engage
in complex cross-modal fusion modules, leading to higher
computational complexity and training challenges. Besides,
these methods generally ignore the effective integration of
historical information, which is crucial to grasping the
change in the target’s appearance and motion trends. Given
the recent advancements in Mamba’s long-range model-
ing and linear complexity, we explore its potential in ad-
dressing the above issues in RGBE tracking tasks. Specif-
ically, we first propose an efficient fusion module based
on Mamba, which utilizes a simple gate-based interaction
scheme to achieve effective modality-selective fusion. This
module can be seamlessly integrated into the encoding layer
of prevalent Transformer-based backbones. Moreover, we
further present a novel historical decoder that leverages
Mamba’s advanced long sequence modeling to effectively
capture the target appearance changes with autoregressive
queries. Extensive experiments show that our proposed ap-
proach achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple
challenging short-term and long-term RGBE benchmarks.
Besides, the effectiveness of each key Mamba-based com-
ponent of our approach is evidenced by our thorough abla-
tion study.Code will be released at: https://github.
com/scy0712/MamTrack
1. Introduction
Visual object tracking (VOT) is a fundamental task in com-
puter vision[21–23, 30, 46] that focuses on estimating the
position and shape of a target within video sequences based
on its initial state [1, 3, 5, 17, 35, 36, 38, 47].Owing to the
advantages of high temporal resolution and dynamic range
offered by event cameras [33, 34, 40], there has been a

growing trend of integrating them with conventional RGB
cameras for robust visual tracking tasks [10, 28, 32, 41–
43, 48]. These RGBE multimodal approaches can signif-
icantly enhance tracking performance in challenging con-
ditions, such as fast motion and limited illumination. Al-
though being effective, the above multimodal methods ex-
pend a substantial amount of labor on developing overly
intricate fusion algorithms. For example, FENet [41] em-
ploys a total of 8 self-attention and 4 complex cross-domain
attention operations to integrate event and frame features
at various levels. Implementing these sophisticated strate-
gies will significantly increase the computational complex-
ity and challenge of the training.
Moreover, the complex fusion designs make existing
RGBE methods usually overlook the mining and applica-
tion of historical temporal information, which is crucial for
tracking as it captures changes in the target’s state. Sev-
eral RGB-only trackers [1, 4, 38] have been developed to
update appearance information by replacing or fusing the
templates. Occasionally, these straightforward methods in-
effectively filter out unreliable updated templates and thus
compromise the performance. To address this issue, some

the Transformer to transfer temporal information across
multiple search frames. However, the Transformer struc-
ture lacks intrinsic designs for temporal sequential model-
ing, resulting in an inherent constraint, particularly in han-
dling long sequences.
Recently, Mamba [11], a novel State Space Model
(SSM) [9, 12, 26, 37], has emerged as a highly promising
approach for efficient long sequence modeling due to con-
volutional computation and linear complexity. Drawing in-
spiration from this advancement, as shown in Figure 1, we
present mamba-based modules to facilitate robust RGB-E
tracking by efficient multimodal fusion and effective histor-
ical information transmission. Specifically, we first propose
an efficient fusion module based on Mamba, which utilizes
a simple gate-based interaction scheme to enhance the rela-
tionship between search and template tokens, as well as the
complementarity between RGB and event modalities. This
module is then easily inserted into the encoding layer of
prevalent transformer-based backbones for combining the
advantages of self-attention.
Furthermore, we present a
novel historical information decoder, which investigates the
great potential of mamba in long sequence modeling to cap-
ture the appearance of targets by introducing a set of addi-
tional autoregressive queries.
Extensive experiments on multiple challenging RGBE
benchmarks show the effectiveness of our approach, which
outperforms existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in
both short-term and long-term tracking (see Figure 2). Ab-
lation studies verify the importance of each key component.
More importantly, we reveal the considerable potential of
Mamba architecture in object tracking tasks. In summary,
we make the following contributions:
• We present a novel and effective framework, dubbed
MamTrack, a pioneering approach to incorporate the
Mamba mechanism into RGBE multimodal tracking
tasks.
• Our proposed Mamba-based fusion module and histori-
cal decoder are capable of adaptively fusing multimodal
information and effectively capturing the historical tem-
poral cues of the target appearance changes, respectively.
• The proposed trackers achieve SOTA performance on
multiple challenging short-term and long-term RGBE
tracking benchmarks.
2. Related Works
2.1. Mamba
The concept of the State Space Model (SSM) was first intro-
duced in the S4 model [12], presenting a distinctive archi-
tecture capable of effectively modeling global information
compared to traditional convolutional neural networks and
Transformers. In their general form, SSM can be written as
follows:
˙x(t) = A(t)x(t) + B(t)u(t),
(1)
y(t) = C(t)x(t) + D(t)u(t).
(2)
This process maps a 1-D input sequence u(t) ∈R to a 1-D
output sequence y(t) ∈R through an implicit N-D latent
state sequence x(t) ∈RN. Building on the S4 model, the
S5 model [26] reduces complexity to a linear level, while
H3 [9] introduces it into language model tasks. Mamba
[11] introduces a data-dependent SSM layer and a selec-
tion mechanism using parallel scan (S6), achieving higher
inference speed and overall metrics compared to equivalent-
scale Transformers. Recently, Mamba has been employed
in discriminative computer vision models and drawn great
attention [7, 14, 18, 20, 49]. For example, ViM [49] ap-
plies Mamba to the Vision Transformer [8] architecture.
VMamba [20] designs a cross-scan mechanism to bridge
the gap between 1-D array scanning and 2-D plain travers-
ing. Unlike previous efforts, we explore a novel architecture
for RGB-E tracking based on Mamba, further unleashing its
potential in visual tasks.
2.2. RGB-Event Single Object Tracking
Recently, due to the unreliable nature of RGB-only data in
challenging scenarios, more and more studies introduced
event cameras to enhance tracking performance.
These
multimodal trackers can be primarily categorised into two
categories based on the vision backbone employed. The
first one [29, 41, 42] utilizes conventional CNNs to extract
features from both RGB and event modalities, followed by
a meticulously designed cross-modal attention mechanism
for fusion. The second approach [28, 32] adopts the Trans-
former as the backbone, leveraging the multi-head attention
mechanism to effectively model the indispensable correla-
tion relationship between the RGB and the event modalities.
To tackle the challenge of limited multimodal tracking data,

The methods mentioned above primarily emphasise mul-
timodal fusion and overlook the significance of mining his-
torical information, which is crucial for multimodal track-
ing. In contrast, we explore the great potential of Mamba
for multimodal tracking tasks. By combining the gating sig-
nals of two modalities in Mamba and leveraging the tempo-
ral modeling mechanism of Mamba, our approach is capa-
ble of concurrently achieving adaptive RGB-E multimodal
fusion and efficient utilization of historical cues.
2.3. Tracking with Historical Temporal Informa-
tion
The historical information can provide valuable insights
into the target’s movements, appearance, and behaviour,
thereby enhancing the tracker’s confidence. Based on the
number of search images input into the tracker, existing
tracking approaches that leverage historical temporal cues
can be categorised into two groups. The first one involves
only inputting one search image and implementing a dy-
namic kernel filter [1, 6, 44] or a specialized update branch
[4, 27, 38] to capture the target appearance changes with
time and dynamically update template images during track-
ing. However, these methods generally involve handcrafted
strategies, requiring tedious tuning for various application
conditions.
Another line of work [25, 35, 36, 47] takes
multiple search sequences as input and then models the se-
quential evolution of target trajectories across frames by
explicitly decoding the entire trajectory sequence step by
step.
Despite these advances, Transformer architectures
employed in these methods are not intrinsically designed for
temporal sequential modeling, which presents an inherent
limitation. Competing with Transformer, Mamba [11] has
shown great potential for long sequence modeling. There-
fore, our research endeavors to design a novel Mamba-
based historical decoder to effectively transmit temporal in-
formation in a parallel training manner.
3. Methodology
The overall architecture of our proposed MamTrack is il-
lustrated in Figure 3, which has two branches with shared
weights: RGB branch and Event branch. Each branch re-
ceives a template and multiple search images as inputs and
corresponding features can be extracted by the Multimodal
Encoder. The core of the Multimodal Encoder is our pro-
posed Fusion Mamba (FM) module, which is inserted be-
tween Transformer encoder layers to leverage the advan-
tages of both RGB and event modalities. In particular, the
RGB modal offers abundant rich texture information, while
the event modal is adept at handling challenging scenarios.
The fused features are then input into our other primary
component, the Historical Encoder, which specifically aims
to capture the target appearance changes and motion trends
by utilizing temporal cues. Finally, the fused features are
multiplied with the decoder’s output and then fed into the
prediction head to locate the targets.

3.2. Fusion Mamba Module
Our proposed Fusion Mamba (FM) module aims to fuse
multimodal semantic information. The key to FM is de-
signed based on the following observations: (i) The inter-
action between template and search features is crucial as
it can help the tracker to learn and prioritize the target-
relevant search features; (ii) Directly combining RGB and
event modals disregards cases where one of modalities can-
not provide valuable cues. In the FM, we present Target-
Aware Scan module (TAS) and Cross-Modality Scan mod-
ule (CMS) to address the above issues, respectively.

3.3. Historical Decoder

tracking as it provides the state changes of targets across
frames. To fully exploit the temporal cues, we propose the
Historical Decoder with M layers, each layer consists of
two key components: Historical State Aware (HSA) module
and Feature Sequence Attention (FSA) module.

3.4. Head and Loss
We employ a center-based head as regular [39] to predict the
center position and scale of the target. The prediction head
outputs include the classification score map, the bounding
box size, and the offset size. We use focal loss [19] and
GIoU loss [24] for training the network. The total loss L is:
L = Lcls + λiouLiou + λL1LL1,
(15)
where Lcls denotes the weighted focal loss for classifi-
cation, the generalized GIoU loss Liou and L1 loss L1
are adopted for bounding box regression, λiou = 2 and
λL1 = 5 are the hyperparameters.
4. Experiments
4.1. Experimental Settings
Implementation Details. We implemented MamTrack us-
ing PyTorch and trained it on 8 NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs
with a batch size of 16. We employed the AdamW op-
timizer with a weight decay of 10−4 and a learning rate
of 4 × 10−4. We utilized pretrained HiViT-Base [45] as
the Transformer encoder with 20 layers. Fine-tuning Mam-
Track on the RGB-Event training set took 50 epochs. Our
proposed Fusion Mamba module is inserted into the 12th,
15th, and 18th layers. The decoder consists of 3 layers (i.e.,
M = 3). Besides, we utilize the Hamming window to in-
corporate positional priors.
Evaluation Metrics. We adopt three widely used met-
rics for quantitatively evaluating the tracking performance:
Success Rate (SR), Precision Rate (PR), and Overlap Preci-
sion (OPT ). The SR focuses on the frame where the overlap
between ground truth and predicted bounding box is larger
than a threshold; OPT matches SR but with a specific over-
lap threshold T. The PR metric counts the frame on which
the center distance between the ground truth and predicted
bounding box is within a given threshold.
4.2. Comparisons with State-of-the-arts
To demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach,
we compare our tracker with representative state-of-the-
art trackers on three widely utilized benchmarks: VisEvent
[29], FELT [31], and FE108 [41].
VisEvent. VisEvent is a large-scale visible-event track-
ing benchmark, which contains 500 training and 320 test-
ing sequences with 17 attributes.
As shown in Figure
5(a), our MamTrack achieves the top SR and PR of 61.6%
and 79.2%, respectively, which beats all single- and multi-
modal SOTA trackers. For example, our method outper-
forms the pure Transformer-based temporal tracker AQA-
Track [36] by 2.9% on SR and multimodal tracker SD-
STrack [13] by 1.9%. Figure 6 further provides the tracking
performance under 17 challenging attributes. We can see

4.3. Ablation Study and Analysis
Impact of Multimodal Input. We assess the effectiveness
of multimodal fusion by separately utlizing event-only and
RGB-only inputs. As shown in Table 2 #1 and #2, the track-
ing results with unimodal input are significantly worse than
those with multimodal input, demonstrating that our method
effectively utilizes both modalities’ advantages to improve
tracking under degraded conditions.
Effectiveness of Fusion Mamba Module. There are two
key mamba-based components in our Fusion Mamba (FM)
module: (i) Target-Aware Scan (TAS) facilitates the inter-
action between the template and search tokens; (ii) Cross-
Modality Scan (CMS) focuses on the fusion of event and
RGB modalities in an adaptive manner. To verify their ef-
fectiveness, we modify the original model by dropping each
of the components and retraining the modified models. The
tracking performance in Table 2 #3 and #4 has shown a de-
crease to varying degrees, indicating the effectiveness and
rationality of our designed FM module. In CMS, the gate-
based operation Cross-Fusion (CF) is the primary operation
that supports the interaction between the two modalities.
We thus eliminate the CF to showcase its indispensability.
#5 shows that when the CF is removed, the SR drops by
1.6%. This illustrates that the deep interaction among fea-
tures from both modalities plays a key role.
One possible factor that impacts the contribution of FM
to our tracker is the location of FM insertion in the encoder.

mance slightly declines. This decrease is due to the limited
number of video sequences used in each iteration, which
impairs the model’s generalization ability.
Effectiveness for Long-term Tracking. To further demon-
strate the effectiveness of our Mamba-based historical de-
coder in capturing temporal information, we analyze its
performance in long-term tracking. Specifically, we evalu-
ate the tracking performance of sequences containing more
than i frames on the VisEvent individually, where i ∈
{300, 500, 700, 1000, 1500, 2000}.
Figure 7 shows that
our MamTrack outperforms other SOTA Transformer-based
temporal trackers and multimodal trackers by a large margin
in SR across all settings. This suggests our Mamba-based
approach proves superior in capturing long-term cues com-
pared to the Transformer-based autoregressive scheme.

4.5. Visualization
We first provide a visual comparison across four challeng-
ing conditions on the VisEvent dataset. As shown in Fig-
ure 8, our approach can accurately track the target under all
conditions. In particular, our method effectively fuses the
advantages of RGB and event to enhance tracker confidence
when the target is in scenes with motion blur or fast motion.
Besides, in situations where the target is partially occluded
or the background is complex, the historical cues encourage
our method to recall the target’s appearance, thereby mini-
mizing environmental interference.
Furthermore, we also visualize the attention maps of the
encoder and decoder to demonstrate the effectiveness of his-
torical information. As shown in Figure 9, guided by histor-
ical information, our MamTrack pays more attention to the
target’s location under challenging conditions.
5. Conclusion
We propose MamTrack, a novel approach jointly leverages
multimodal spatial and historical temporal information for
RGBE object tracking. Our historical decoder, based on
the innovative Mamba architecture, effectively captures tar-
get appearance changes and motion trends, enabling the
model to locate the target within complex backgrounds. We
also introduce a simple yet effective Mamba-based fusion
method for integrating cross-modality cues. Extensive eval-
uations demonstrate that our method achieves competitive
performance compared to previous SOTA trackers. How-
ever, we primarily focuses on the effectiveness of Mamba
in modality fusion, but not leverage the high temporal reso-
lution characteristics of event data. Future research will ex-
plore this aspect to enhance the performance of the tracker.
